q: Which of these is a valid storage account name?
exp: Storage account names must be 3–24 characters long, use only lowercase letters and numbers, and be globally unique because they become part of the URL. contosodata01 fits. 'Contoso-Data' has a capital letter and a hyphen, 'contoso_data' has an underscore, and 'cd' is too short.

q: What is the blob endpoint format of a storage account named contosodata?
exp: Each storage service has an endpoint in the form https://<account>.<service>.core.windows.net, so the blob endpoint is https://contosodata.blob.core.windows.net. azurewebsites.net is for App Service.

q: Which CLI command creates a GPv2 account with ZRS?
opts: az storage account create -n st1 -g RG1 --sku Standard_ZRS --kind StorageV2
az storage account new -n st1 -g RG1 --redundancy zone --kind BlobStorage
exp: az storage account create uses --sku to set performance and redundancy together, so Standard_ZRS means a standard account with zone-redundant storage. --kind StorageV2 makes it general-purpose v2. The other commands don't exist.

q: You need a data lake with true directories, atomic directory renames, and POSIX ACLs. What do you enable when creating the account?
exp: Enabling hierarchical namespace turns the account into Data Lake Storage Gen2: real directories, atomic renames and moves of whole directories, and POSIX-style access control lists. Large file shares, NFS and versioning don't give you directories or ACLs.

q: An old GPv1 account needs access tiers and lifecycle management. What should you do?
exp: GPv1 accounts don't support access tiers or lifecycle management. You can upgrade a GPv1 account to GPv2 in place, without moving data or downtime, but you can't go back. Recreating as premium would remove tiering, and versioning or moving region don't change the account kind.

q: How many storage accounts can you create per region per subscription by default?
exp: By default you can create 250 storage accounts per region per subscription, and you can ask support to raise it (up to 500). If you need many more, spread accounts across regions or subscriptions. It isn't 50 or unlimited.

q: Which premium account type gives the best performance for workloads with high transaction rates on small objects?
exp: Premium BlockBlobStorage accounts use SSDs and are built for high transaction rates and low latency on blobs, especially many small objects. Standard GPv2 hot and cool use HDD-based storage, and FileStorage is for file shares rather than blobs.

q: You must host a static website (HTML/JS) directly from storage. What do you enable?
opts: Static website hosting, which serves the $web container
Anonymous access, which publishes the $root container
exp: Static website hosting on a storage account serves files from a special $web container through a website endpoint, with an index page and an error page. Anonymous container access only exposes blob URLs. Azure Files and a CDN on their own don't host a website.

q: Which redundancy option protects against a single availability zone outage without replicating to another region?
exp: ZRS copies data synchronously to three availability zones in the same region, so it keeps working if one zone fails and the data never leaves the region. LRS stays in one datacenter, while GRS and RA-GRS replicate to another region.

q: The lowest-cost redundancy option is:
exp: LRS keeps three copies in one datacenter, so it's the cheapest option but gives the least protection. ZRS (three zones), GRS (a second region) and GZRS (both) each cost more because they store data in more places.

q: Which property tells you how far behind the secondary region is in a GRS or RA-GRS account?
exp: Last Sync Time is a property of geo-redundant accounts. Everything written before that time is guaranteed to be in the secondary region; anything written after it may not be yet. Check it before a failover to judge how much data could be lost. Change feed and blob inventory don't report replication progress.

q: An app uses RA-GRS. What's the endpoint for reading from the secondary blob service of account st1?
exp: With RA-GRS or RA-GZRS, every service gets a secondary endpoint: the account name plus -secondary, for example https://st1-secondary.blob.core.windows.net. Applications read from it when the primary is unavailable. The other formats don't exist.

q: Which redundancy gives the highest durability and availability, including read access during a regional outage?
exp: RA-GZRS keeps three copies across zones in the primary region (surviving a zone failure), copies data to the paired region (surviving a region outage), and lets you read the secondary copy at any time. GRS lacks zone redundancy and read access, ZRS stays in one region, and LRS stays in one datacenter.

q: Why can account failover on a GRS account cause data loss?
opts: Replication to the secondary is asynchronous, so recent writes may not have been copied
GRS is synchronous, so writes that were in progress during the failover are rolled back
exp: Geo-replication to the secondary region is asynchronous: writes are acknowledged once they're stored in the primary region, and copied a little later. If you fail over, anything written after the Last Sync Time may be missing from the secondary. Failover doesn't deliberately delete data, and GRS isn't synchronous.

q: You change an account from LRS to ZRS. How is this done?
opts: Through a conversion (customer-initiated in the portal, or migration)
Instantly from the redundancy dropdown, with no data being copied
Only by creating a new tenant
exp: Changing to or from zone redundancy (LRS ↔ ZRS) needs a conversion, which you start in the portal (or a manual migration), and it takes time because data is redistributed across zones. Adding geo-redundancy (LRS → GRS) is a simple setting change.

q: Which TWO redundancy options keep a copy in a secondary region?
exp: GRS and GZRS (and their read-access versions RA-GRS and RA-GZRS) copy data to a secondary paired region. LRS keeps data in one datacenter, and ZRS keeps it across zones in a single region.

q: Answer Yes or No:
stmts: GRS keeps 6 copies of data in total
ZRS protects against a full region outage
The secondary region for GRS is chosen by you freely
RA-GRS lets you read the secondary without failover
exp: GRS keeps 6 copies: 3 in the primary region and 3 in the secondary. ZRS stays within one region, so it doesn't protect against a region outage. You can't choose the secondary region — it's the paired region. RA-GRS lets you read the secondary at any time without a failover.

q: An app must stay available even if one datacenter in the region fails, and data residency rules forbid leaving the region. Choose:
exp: ZRS stores three synchronous copies in three availability zones (separate datacenters) of the same region. If one datacenter fails, the data is still available, and it never leaves the region. GRS, RA-GRS and GZRS all copy data to another region, which breaks the residency requirement.

q: Which blob types does object replication support?
exp: Object replication copies block blobs asynchronously from a source account to a destination account. It only supports block blobs: page blobs (used for VM disks) and append blobs (used for logs) can't be replicated, so 'all blob types' is wrong.

q: In an object replication policy, which filter limits replication to blobs whose names start with 'invoices/'?
exp: Object replication rules can include a prefix match filter, for example 'invoices/', so only blobs whose names start with that text are replicated. You can also filter by creation time. Tags, tiers and lifecycle rules don't scope replication.

q: Can blobs in the archive tier be replicated by object replication?
opts: Only when the account uses RA-GRS
exp: Blobs in the archive tier aren't replicated by object replication, because archived data is offline. Rehydrate them to an online tier first if they need to be replicated. Redundancy and the 180-day minimum don't change this.

q: In object replication, what does the destination container become?
exp: While an object replication policy is in place, the destination container is read-only for clients; only the replication process writes to it. This keeps the copy consistent with the source. To write to it again, remove the policy.

q: Order the steps to configure object replication from st-src to st-dst:
items: Create the replication policy and rules on st-dst / st-src
Enable blob versioning on both accounts
Upload a test blob and verify replication status
exp: Object replication needs versioning on both accounts and change feed on the source, so turn those on first. Then create the replication policy and its rules. Finally upload a test blob and check its replication status. Creating the policy before the prerequisites fails.

q: Which encryption algorithm does Azure Storage SSE use?
exp: Azure Storage encrypts all data at rest with 256-bit AES, one of the strongest block ciphers available, and it's FIPS 140-2 compliant. DES is weak and obsolete, RSA is asymmetric (not used for bulk data), and MD5 is a hash, not encryption.

q: Where can a customer-managed key for Azure Storage be stored?
opts: Azure Key Vault or Key Vault Managed HSM
A container in the same storage account
exp: Customer-managed keys for Azure Storage must be kept in Azure Key Vault or Azure Key Vault Managed HSM. The storage account reaches the key through a managed identity. Keys can't be stored in a storage account, App Service or Entra ID.

q: Compliance requires that the customer, not Microsoft, controls key rotation and can revoke access to all storage data. What do you configure?
exp: With customer-managed keys in Key Vault, you own the key: you control when it rotates, and you can disable or delete it to cut off access to all data in the account. With Microsoft-managed keys, Microsoft rotates them and you can't revoke access that way. Infrastructure encryption and secure transfer don't give you key control.

q: A client must encrypt data on its side before uploading, so Azure never sees plaintext. Which approach?
exp: Client-side encryption (available in the Azure Storage client libraries) encrypts data inside your application before it's uploaded, so Azure only ever stores and sees ciphertext. Server-side encryption and infrastructure encryption happen in Azure after the data arrives, and secure transfer only protects data in transit.

q: Which AzCopy command copies a blob directly between two storage accounts (server-to-server)?
exp: When both source and destination are storage URLs, azcopy copy uses server-to-server copy: the data moves directly between the storage accounts, not through your computer. azcopy move and azcopy transfer don't exist, and sync with --local isn't valid.

q: Which AzCopy option copies a folder and all its subfolders?
exp: --recursive tells AzCopy to include every file in the folder and all its subfolders. Without it, AzCopy only copies the files at the top level of the folder. --all, --deep and --include-subdirs aren't AzCopy options.

q: An AzCopy job was interrupted halfway. How do you continue it without restarting?
exp: AzCopy saves a plan file for every job. If a job stops part-way, azcopy jobs resume <job-id> continues from where it stopped instead of starting again. Find the job ID with azcopy jobs list. Copying again with --overwrite would re-transfer files.

q: azcopy sync with --delete-destination=true does what?
opts: Deletes files at the destination that no longer exist at the source
Deletes files at the source after they have been copied successfully
exp: With --delete-destination=true, azcopy sync also deletes files at the destination that no longer exist at the source, so the destination becomes an exact mirror. By default sync only copies new and changed files and never deletes. It doesn't touch the source.

q: Which AzCopy command signs in with an Entra identity?
exp: azcopy login signs AzCopy in with Microsoft Entra ID, either interactively or with --identity for a managed identity or with a service principal. After that, you don't need SAS tokens in your URLs. The other commands don't exist.

q: You sign in with azcopy login. What role must your identity have to upload blobs?
exp: With Entra ID sign-in, uploading blobs is a data-plane operation, so your identity needs a data role such as Storage Blob Data Contributor or Storage Blob Data Owner. Reader, Contributor and Storage Account Contributor are control-plane roles and don't grant data access on their own.

q: Which ways can Storage Explorer connect to storage?
opts: Entra sign-in, account name and key, SAS URL, connection string
Only Entra sign-in with the Owner role on the subscription
exp: Storage Explorer can connect by signing in with Microsoft Entra ID, by account name and key, by a SAS URL, by a connection string, and to the local Azurite emulator. It isn't limited to one method and doesn't need the portal.

q: What does Storage Explorer use internally for fast upload and download transfers?
exp: Storage Explorer uses AzCopy behind the scenes for uploads, downloads and copies between accounts, which gives it fast, parallel transfers. Robocopy, FTP and rsync aren't used, and you can also run AzCopy yourself for scripted transfers.

q: About 40 TB must be moved to Azure from a site with a slow internet link. Which option is designed for this?
opts: Azure Data Box (an appliance shipped to the site)
AzCopy over the existing internet link
exp: Data Box is an offline transfer appliance: you copy data to it on site and ship it to Microsoft, which avoids weeks of uploading over a slow link. AzCopy, File Sync and Storage Explorer all depend on the network.

q: For the Azure Import/Export service, which tool prepares drives for import?
exp: For the Azure Import/Export service you prepare drives with the WAImportExport tool. It copies data to the disks, encrypts them with BitLocker, and creates the journal files Azure needs to import the data. AzCopy and Storage Explorer transfer data over the network instead.

q: An analytics team needs a daily CSV listing all blobs with their tier and size for reports. Which feature?
exp: Blob inventory runs on a daily or weekly schedule and writes a CSV or Parquet report listing your blobs with properties such as tier, size and last modified time. Change feed records changes rather than listing the current state, and lifecycle management moves data without reporting on it.

q: You need an ordered, durable log of every blob create, update, and delete for auditing and downstream processing. Which feature?
exp: Change feed is an ordered, durable, read-only log of every create, update and delete on the blobs in an account, kept in the account itself. Applications can read it for auditing or to trigger processing. Soft delete, versioning and snapshots keep old data, but they aren't an event log.

q: Which setting can ONLY be chosen when a storage account is created?
opts: Default access tier of the account
exp: Infrastructure encryption — a second layer of encryption below the service level — can only be turned on when the storage account is created. The default access tier, firewall rules and minimum TLS version can all be changed later.

q: Which setting can be changed after a storage account is created?
opts: Account kind from FileStorage to BlockBlobStorage
exp: You can switch the default access tier between hot, cool and cold at any time (and smart on zone-redundant accounts). The performance tier (Standard or Premium), the premium account kind and the account name are fixed once the account is created — you'd need a new account and to copy the data.

q: You must move a storage account from West Europe to North Europe. Supported approach?
opts: Create a new account in North Europe and copy the data to it
Use object replication and then start an account failover
exp: A storage account can't change region. To move it, create a new account in North Europe (you can export the original's template to copy its settings), copy the data with AzCopy or similar, point applications to the new account, and then delete the old one. There's no region property or move command.

q: Which metric helps detect throttling on a storage account?
opts: Used capacity filtered by access tier
exp: When an account is throttled, requests fail with errors such as ServerBusyError. Split the Transactions metric by the ResponseType dimension to see how many requests returned throttling errors. Capacity, ingress and blob count don't show throttling.

q: How do you send storage blob read, write, and delete logs to Log Analytics?
opts: Create a diagnostic setting on the blob service
Install the Azure Monitor Agent on the account
exp: Storage resource logs (StorageRead, StorageWrite, StorageDelete) are sent through a diagnostic setting created on the specific service, such as blob, with a Log Analytics workspace as the destination. Soft delete and versioning protect data, and storage accounts don't run an agent.

q: Which statement about tier costs is correct?
opts: Hot has the highest storage cost and lowest access cost
Archive has the highest storage cost and no access cost
exp: Moving from hot to cool, cold and archive lowers the storage price per GB but raises the cost of accessing data. Hot is cheapest to read and most expensive to store; archive is cheapest to store but expensive and slow to read back. Every tier except hot also charges per GB read.

q: Data is read frequently for 2 weeks and then rarely touched but must stay instantly available for a year. Cheapest correct approach?
opts: Upload to hot, then a lifecycle rule moves it to cool (or cold) after 14 days
Upload directly to archive, then a lifecycle rule moves it to hot when it's read
Keep in hot for a year
exp: Hot is cheapest to access, which suits the first 2 weeks. After that, cool or cold is cheaper to store and still online, so data is instantly available. A lifecycle rule moves it automatically. Archive would make the data offline, and premium or hot for a year costs more.

q: Which PowerShell cmdlet creates a storage account?
exp: New-AzStorageAccount creates a storage account (with -ResourceGroupName, -Name, -Location, -SkuName and -Kind). Set-AzStorageAccount changes an existing one. New-AzStorage and Add-AzStorageAccount don't exist.

q: You enable 'Allow cross-tenant replication = false'. What is affected?
opts: Object replication policies can't use accounts in other Entra tenants
Geo-replication to a paired region in another geography stops working
exp: 'Allow cross-tenant replication' = false stops object replication policies from using a source or destination account in another Microsoft Entra tenant. It doesn't affect geo-replication (GRS), private endpoints or SAS.

ctx: An application writes telemetry blobs at very high rates and needs single-digit millisecond latency. Data loss of a zone is acceptable, but cost must be reasonable.
q: Which account configuration fits best?
exp: Premium BlockBlobStorage uses SSDs for single-digit millisecond latency and very high transaction rates, which suits heavy telemetry ingestion. LRS keeps the cost down, and losing a zone's worth of resilience is acceptable here. Standard GPv2 is slower, archive is offline, and FileStorage is for file shares.

ctx: Account st1: Standard GPv2, RA-GZRS, versioning on, change feed on, CMK in Key Vault (soft delete + purge protection).
q: Answer Yes or No:
stmts: st1 can be the source of an object replication policy
st1 survives a zone outage in the primary region with no data loss
Disabling the key in Key Vault blocks reads of st1 data
st1 can be converted to Premium performance in place
exp: Versioning (with change feed) meets the object replication source requirements. RA-GZRS writes synchronously across zones, so a zone outage loses no data. With customer-managed keys, disabling the key blocks access to the data. Standard to Premium can't be changed in place.
